title: US Denies Iran's Claims of Destroying F-35 Jets as Conflict Escalates
excerpt: CENTCOM says all Iranian missiles were intercepted after IRGC claimed ballistic missile strikes destroyed American fighter jets at a Jordan air base, while the US and Saudi Arabia jointly struck Iran-backed groups in Iraq.
body:
• Iran's IRGC claimed it destroyed three US F-35 fighter jets at Al Azraq Air Base in Jordan; CENTCOM denied any aircraft were damaged
  • The US resumed strikes inside Iran on July 29, targeting military command centers, drone storage facilities, and maritime capabilities
  • Saudi Arabia publicly joined US forces for the first time in striking Iran-backed groups in Iraq, killing at least 20 militia members
  • An AP-NORC poll found two-thirds of Americans say the nearly six-month-old conflict with Iran is "not worth fighting"

The US military flatly denied Iran's claim that its ballistic missile strikes destroyed American fighter jets at a base in Jordan, as Washington and Tehran traded fresh attacks that ended a brief pause in the nearly six-month-old conflict.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said its Aerospace Force attacked Al Azraq Air Base and CENTCOM headquarters in Jordan with ballistic missiles, claiming it destroyed three F-35 fighter jets and heavily damaged three others. US Central Command dismissed the assertion entirely.

“All missiles and drones were intercepted or failed to reach targeted areas.”

— US Central Command, statement on X

A ‘Surprise Attack’ Shatters the Pause

The IRGC launched multiple ballistic missiles at US forces at approximately 5:45 p.m. Eastern Time on Tuesday, July 29 — what CENTCOM called an “attempted surprise attack.” The strike shattered a pause in fighting that began when President Donald Trump halted 13 consecutive nights of US bombing inside Iran on July 25 to allow diplomacy another chance.

Jordan's military confirmed it intercepted and destroyed five Iranian missiles, with no immediate reports of casualties or damage. The attack followed a deadlier Iranian strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan earlier in July that killed two US service members and wounded several others.

Iran said the latest attack was in retaliation for a US strike on Iran's Qeshm Island that killed two parents and a child, according to the official Islamic Republic News Agency.

US Responds With Strikes Inside Iran

The United States resumed airstrikes inside Iran on the night of July 29, targeting what CENTCOM described as “military command centers, drone storage facilities, communication networks, coastal surveillance sites, and maritime capabilities.” Trump had telegraphed the retaliation hours earlier.

“We’re going to be hitting them very hard because it’s our turn to hit them. We got to smack them a little bit.”

— President Donald Trump, Oval Office remarks, July 29

The IRGC also struck US assets in Kuwait, claiming it destroyed two drone hangars and a fuel storage facility at Ali Al Salem Air Base using what it called “advanced and ultra-heavy” kamikaze drones. Iran's foreign minister, Sayed Aragchi, confirmed on social media that Iran had been “launching Ballistic Missile strikes at American Bases in Kuwait and Jordan for the past several hours.”

Saudi Arabia Enters the Fight Publicly

In a significant shift, Saudi Arabia publicly joined US forces on July 29 to strike Iran-backed armed groups in eastern Iraq. CENTCOM said US and Saudi fighter aircraft hit “multiple terrorist logistics and weapons sites” in response to more than 30 IRGC-directed drone attacks over 72 hours. Iraq's Popular Mobilization Forces, aligned with Iran, said at least 20 of its members were killed, according to the BBC.

The joint US-Saudi operation marked the first time Riyadh openly acknowledged participating in strikes alongside Washington in this conflict. Saudi Arabia's involvement came after drone attacks launched from Iraq hit Saudi oil facilities, with the Saudi Defence Ministry warning it “does not seek escalation but will respond to any aggression.”

Competing Factions Inside Tehran

The Washington-based Institute for the Study of War reported that Iran's intransigence is driven by internal power struggles. Three competing groups within the regime are attempting to shape negotiations: the IRGC, led by Maj. Gen. Ahmad Vahidi, pushing for control of the Strait of Hormuz while engaging in talks; a pro-compromise group including President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Aragchi; and the ultra-hardline Paydari Front, which opposes all negotiations with the US.

Behnam Ben Taleblu of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies warned that Iran's willingness to launch surprise attacks reflects a dangerous strategic shift. “This is the Islamic Republic matching its deeds with its words. That means a more risk-tolerant, more confident, perhaps less capable, but more dangerous Iran,” he told Fox News.

Strait of Hormuz Remains the Sticking Point

Control of the Strait of Hormuz — which carried 20% of the world's oil before the war — remains the central dispute. Iran rejected an Omani proposal for joint regional management of the waterway, insisting on broader control over shipping routes. For India, which sources a significant share of its crude oil from the Persian Gulf, the disruption to maritime traffic through the strait continues to raise energy security concerns.

Trump, who signed a preliminary peace deal with Iran in June, acknowledged on Fox News that “Iran took a beating over the last 14 days and they asked us very nicely, ‘Please stop, let’s meet.’” But the AP-NORC poll released this week found that two-thirds of US adults — including large majorities of Democrats and independents — believe the war was “not worth fighting.” Trump's approval rating stood at roughly 33%.

With the conflict now in its sixth month, the cycle of strikes and counter-strikes shows no signs of breaking. “You have to treat every single Iranian missile attack, whether it was successful or not, as being successful,” Ben Taleblu said. “This is not a technological problem. This is a political problem.”
